verdicts.trueWording: experts reached moderate-to-substantial agreement, whereas lay judges remained inconsistent
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML (2601.18353v1), Findings 4.1: 'Inter-annotator agreement also differed: experts reached moderate-to-substantial agreement (kappa=0.41-0.67 for Writing Quality; kappa=0.54-0.58 for Stylistic Fidelity), whereas lay judges remained inconsistent (kappa=0.07-0.22).' Quote appears word for word; both limbs (expert moderate-to-substantial, lay inconsistent) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: their preference for AI writing triggered an identity crisis, eroding aesthetic confidence
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML abstract (2601.18353v1): 'Debrief interviews with expert writers revealed that their preference for AI writing triggered an identity crisis, eroding aesthetic confidence and questioning what constitutes “good writing.”' Quote verbatim; every limb (debrief interviews, expert writers, identity crisis, eroded aesthetic confidence) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Fine-tuned outputs were rarely flagged as AI-generated (3% vs. 97% for prompting) by leading detectors
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv abs page (2510.13939, v4 last revised 17 Mar 2026, Chakrabarty/Ginsburg/Dhillon). Quote verbatim in the abstract; the 3% fine-tuned / 97% prompting split and the 'leading detectors' attribution are both on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: the median fine-tuning cost of $81 per author represents a 99.7% reduction
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv abs page (2510.13939v4). Quote 'median fine-tuning cost of $81 per author' appears word for word in the abstract.

verdicts.trueWording: In blind pairwise evaluations by 28 MFA-trained readers and 516 college-educated general readers
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv abs page (2510.13939v4). Quote verbatim; both participant counts and both reader categories are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: the AI-written texts received slightly higher average ratings and were more frequently preferred
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv abs page (2601.17363v3) plus the accepted PDF (extracted text): quote verbatim in the abstract, and the Discussion gives the comparator explicitly — Moravia's story (Oval) 6.83 vs the two AI texts 7.33 and 7.42 out of 10, 'While the SynTs slightly outperformed the human-authored one on average, the differences were modest.' Blind setup and Italian language both stated.

verdicts.trueWording: 20 participants read and evaluated three stories, two created with ChatGPT-4o and one by Alberto Moravia
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv abs page (2601.17363v3). Quote verbatim; the three-story stimulus set and its 2 AI / 1 Moravia composition are stated in the abstract and confirmed in the PDF body (Moravia's 'L'incosciente' from Racconti romani).

verdicts.trueWording: LLM-generated stories pass 3-10X less TTCW tests than stories written by professionals
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv abs page (2309.14556v3). Quote verbatim; the same abstract defines TTCW as the Torrance Test of Creative Writing, so every limb of the claim is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: none of the LLMs positively correlate with the expert assessments
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv abs page (2309.14556v3): 'we explore the use of LLMs as assessors to automate the TTCW evaluation, revealing that none of the LLMs positively correlate with the expert assessments.' Quote verbatim; the assessor role is explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: these writers agree on undesirable idiosyncrasies in LLM generated text, formalizing it into a seven-category taxonomy
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv abs page (2409.14509v5): 'we hired professional writers to edit paragraphs in several creative domains. We first found these writers agree on undesirable idiosyncrasies in LLM generated text, formalizing it into a seven-category taxonomy (e.g. clichés, unnecessary exposition).' Quote verbatim; hiring, agreement and formalisation all supported.

verdicts.trueWording: none of the LLMs used in our study outperform each other in terms of writing quality, revealing common limitations across model families
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv abs page (2409.14509v5). Quote verbatim; the sentence names the LAMP corpus as the analysed data and states the 'common limitations across model families' reading, matching both limbs.

verdicts.trueWording: A large-scale preference annotation confirms that although experts largely prefer text edited by other experts
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv abs page (2409.14509v5) for the verbatim quote; the comparator limb ('over automatically edited text') is confirmed in the raw HTML full text (2409.14509v5) conclusion: 'writers consistently rank text edited by other writers highest, followed by LLM-edited text, with unedited LLM-generated text ranking lowest.'

verdicts.trueWording: access to generative AI ideas causes stories to be evaluated as more creative
verdicts.note: Raw Europe PMC JATS full text (PMC11244532, Science Advances 10, eadn5290, 12 July 2024). Quote verbatim in the abstract; 'more creative' is the first listed evaluation outcome.

verdicts.trueWording: generative AI-enabled stories are more similar to each other than stories by humans alone
verdicts.note: Raw Europe PMC JATS full text (PMC11244532). Quote verbatim in the abstract; the Results section corroborates with per-condition similarity coefficients (b=0.871, P<0.001; b=0.718, P=0.003).

verdicts.trueWording: writers in the Human with five GenAI ideas condition show an increase in novelty of 8.1%
verdicts.note: Raw Europe PMC JATS full text (PMC11244532), Results: '...an increase in novelty of 8.1% (b = 0.311, P < 0.001) over writers without generative AI access.' Quote verbatim; the five-ideas condition and the no-AI-access baseline are both named in the same sentence.
